title: The Wise Woman of Tekoa and Absalom's Return
summary: Seeing that David longs for Absalom, Joab sends a wise woman from Tekoa to the king with a made-up case: a widow whose one remaining son killed his brother and whose clan now demands his life. When David promises to protect the son, she turns the ruling on him and urges him to bring back his own banished son. David sees Joab's hand behind it but allows Absalom to return, though he refuses to see him for two years, until Absalom forces Joab's help by burning his field and the king finally receives him with a kiss.
story: Chapter 13 ended with Absalom in exile in Geshur and David longing for him. This chapter brings Absalom home, but only halfway. David neither punishes him for Amnon's murder nor fully restores him; he lets him back into Jerusalem and then keeps him at a distance. The result is two years of resentment, and the kiss that closes the chapter looks like reconciliation without any real reckoning. The very next chapter shows Absalom using his freedom to steal the hearts of Israel. The chapter is a study in how unresolved wrongs in a family can grow into public disaster.
historical:
Tekoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem, later known as the home of the prophet Amos. Joab, David's nephew and commander, is once again the man working behind the scenes, as he did in arranging Uriah's death. His motives are not stated. He may have seen that David's paralysis over Absalom was harming the kingdom, since Absalom was now the likely heir, or he may have been positioning himself with the future king.

The chapter's note that Absalom had three sons (verse 27) sits uneasily with 18:18, where Absalom says he has no son to carry on his name. Many interpreters conclude that the sons died young, which would also explain why they are not named. His daughter bears the name of his wronged sister Tamar. Absalom's yearly haircut weighed two hundred shekels by the royal standard; if the shekel was about eleven or twelve grams, that is more than two kilograms, though the value of the royal shekel is uncertain.
cultural:
Two institutions stand behind the woman's story. The first is blood vengeance. In Israel, as in much of the ancient world, the nearest male relative of a murdered person had the duty to avenge his death. The law called him the avenger of blood and set up cities of refuge to prevent killings in cases of accidental death (Numbers 35; Deuteronomy 19). The second is the importance of preserving a family line. If the widow's last son were killed, her husband's name would vanish, and his land would pass out of the family. Her image of her son as “my one remaining ember” (verse 7) captures that fear. The king, as the highest judge, could intervene to protect the son.

Wise women appear elsewhere in Samuel (a wise woman of Abel saves her city in 20:16-22). They seem to have been respected figures whose counsel and skill with words could shape events. Mourning customs included wearing special clothing and not anointing oneself with oil, the ordinary care for skin and hair in a dry climate.
literary: The woman's appeal works like Nathan's parable in chapter 12. A made-up legal case draws the king into a ruling, and then the ruling is turned back on him. The echo is deliberate: both stories involve a king judging himself without knowing it. But the two cases differ sharply. Nathan confronted David with sin; this woman persuades him to overlook it. Her speech (verses 13-17) is the literary high point, moving from flattery to theology and back again. The chapter then closes with a scene that reverses the opening. David “longed for Absalom” at the start, but when Absalom returns David refuses to see his face, and the repeated phrase about seeing the king's face (verses 24, 28, 32) builds to the final kiss.

outline.t: Joab recruits the wise woman of Tekoa
The widow's case and David's ruling
The woman turns the ruling on the king
David sees Joab's hand and brings Absalom back, but not to his presence
Absalom burns Joab's field and is received by the king

doctrines.note: The woman's words in verse 14, that God “devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him,” are among the most striking statements of grace in the historical books. Although spoken to manipulate, they express a true longing: that God finds a way to bring exiles home.

The chapter shows wisdom as skill with words and persuasion, used here for a mixed purpose. Wisdom in Scripture is not only cleverness; the question is whether it serves what is right. This woman's wisdom works, but it serves Joab's plan more than justice.
David's half-reconciliation with Absalom, bringing him home but refusing to see him, shows how unresolved conflict festers. Neither justice nor genuine forgiveness is pursued, and the damage grows.

words.note: Nadach, to banish or drive out. It describes Absalom's exile (verses 13-14) and God's purpose that the banished one not be cast out. The word is used elsewhere for sheep scattered from the flock (Ezekiel 34:4, 16) and for Israel driven into exile (Deuteronomy 30:4), and the prophets promise that God will gather the banished.

Gaal, to redeem, here in the form avenger of blood (verse 11). The same root names the kinsman-redeemer who buys back land or marries a widow (as Boaz does in Ruth). The go'el was the family's protector, whose duty was to restore what was lost, including by avenging a killing.

Chashav, to think, plan, or devise. The woman uses it twice: the king has devised a thing against God's people (verse 13), but God devises ways to bring back the banished (verse 14). The contrast is between human schemes and divine purposes.

Nashaq, to kiss. The chapter ends with the king kissing Absalom (verse 33). A kiss could signal welcome, reconciliation, or homage, but the narrator records no words between father and son, and the next chapter shows how empty this reconciliation was.

christ: The woman of Tekoa's words in verse 14, “He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him,” have long been read by Christians as a statement of the gospel's logic, though the woman spoke them for a different purpose. The New Testament's answer to how God brings back the banished without ignoring justice is the cross, where God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Absalom's return is the opposite: an exile brought back with neither repentance nor atonement, and the result is rebellion. The contrast is thematic, not a prediction, but it helps a reader see why reconciliation that skips justice cannot hold, and why the gospel insists on both.

hard.q: Was David right to bring Absalom back?
hard.a: Interpreters differ. Some see David's decision as mercy, a father's love overcoming the demand for justice, and point to the woman's appeal to God's own desire to restore the banished. Others see it as a failure of justice. Absalom had committed murder, showed no repentance, and was never held accountable, so David's decision was driven by longing rather than right judgment. The law of Moses did not allow a ransom for a murderer (Numbers 35:31). The narrator gives clues that the second reading is closer to the text's view: the woman's case is fictional and manipulative, David's response is half-hearted, and Absalom's return leads straight to revolt. At the same time the chapter does not condemn the desire for reconciliation itself. The problem is not that David wanted his son back, but that neither justice nor real repentance was part of the return.

questions: The woman said that God “devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him.” Where have you seen God make a way back for someone?
David brought Absalom home but refused to see him. What happens when reconciliation is incomplete?
Joab used the woman's story to move David. When is persuasion wise, and when does it become manipulation?
